summary: Defines the first Management Information Base for TCP/IP network management, the list of things a device can report. It is a re-release of RFC 1066 with technical content unchanged. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1156 defines a set of information that network management software can read from TCP/IP systems. The objects cover system details, interfaces, and IP, ICMP, TCP, UDP, and EGP activity.

subtitle: The initial set of objects for monitoring and controlling TCP/IP networks.

tldr.problem: Network operators needed a shared set of variables for monitoring and controlling TCP/IP systems from different vendors.
tldr.mechanism: The Internet MIB defines objects in eight groups, with each object assigned a name, data type, meaning, access mode, and status.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1156 is Historic. It re-released RFC 1066 with technical content unchanged.

today: RFC 1156 is listed as Historic. It re-released RFC 1066 with its technical content unchanged, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates RFC 1156.

sections.title: The Internet Management Framework
sections.content:
RFC 1156 provides an initial Management Information Base (MIB) for managing TCP/IP-based internets. It is a re-release of RFC 1066 with changes to its status, IAB policy statement, and introduction; the technical content is unchanged.

The framework has three parts: RFC 1155 describes how managed objects are defined, this memo specifies which objects are in the MIB, and RFC 1157 defines the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) used to manage them. The IAB recommended that IP and TCP implementations be network-manageable.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB lists information a management system can access. A separate document defines how the objects are described, and another defines the SNMP protocol used to manage them.

sections.title: Why the MIB Includes These Objects
sections.content:
The authors selected objects considered essential for fault or configuration management. They sought evidence of current use, avoided values that could be derived from other objects, excluded implementation-specific values, and aimed to keep the total near 100 objects so vendors could instrument their software.

Only weak control objects were allowed. The RFC explains that the management protocols available at the time were not secure enough for more powerful control operations. An implementation must support all objects in a group when that group applies to it, but not every group applies to every system.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB focuses on a limited set of useful values. The authors restricted control objects because the management protocols available at the time could not safely support stronger controls.

sections.title: How a Managed Object Is Defined
sections.content:
The MIB is a virtual information store. It defines objects using Abstract Syntax Notation One (ASN.1), with restrictions intended to keep the notation simple. Each object has a name and identifier, a syntax that describes its data, and an encoding for network transmission.

Each object definition also gives its meaning, access mode, and status. Access may be read-only, read-write, write-only, or not-accessible. Status may be mandatory, optional, or obsolete. The definition's meaning should be consistent across implementations from different vendors.
sections.plainLanguage: Each MIB object has an identifier, a data type, a description, and rules for access. These definitions let different systems report the same value in the same way.

sections.title: The Eight Object Groups
sections.content:
The MIB places objects in eight groups: System, Interfaces, Address Translation, IP, ICMP, TCP, UDP, and EGP. The groups provide identifiers and tell implementations which objects apply. For example, the EGP group applies when a system implements EGP, and the TCP group applies to systems that implement TCP.

The System group is mandatory for all systems. It includes a description, an object identifier for the management subsystem, and sysUpTime, which measures time since that subsystem was reinitialized in hundredths of a second. Other groups contain interface counters, IP and ICMP statistics, TCP connection data, UDP counts, and EGP neighbor information.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB groups related information by system function. A system reports every object in each group that applies to it, while the System group applies to all systems.

sections.title: Extending the MIB
sections.content: The MIB can grow through new standard versions, widely available non-standard objects in the multilateral subtree, and private objects in the enterprises subtree. The RFC says these mechanisms can support vendor-specific objects and experimentation. Additional groups and variables were expected to be defined over time.
sections.plainLanguage: New MIB objects can be added through standard updates or separate identifier branches. The RFC expected the set of groups and variables to grow over time.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The Security Considerations section says security issues are not discussed. Earlier, the RFC explains that it limited control objects because the management protocols of the time were not secure enough for more powerful operations.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC does not analyze security. It limited the control objects because the management protocols available at the time did not provide enough security for more powerful operations.
